notes: The difficult verb can concern being cut off or making gain. Either way, Job asks what hope remains when God takes life.
These lines resemble the friends’ descriptions of the wicked. The received text gives no new speaker; the draft keeps them in Job’s speech.
“Will not be gathered” is a difficult expression. It may concern burial, gathering wealth, or no longer doing so. The draft leaves the image unresolved.
The east wind can remain the subject of these personified actions; God or other people have also been understood as the agents.
vocabulary: An image of a fragile dwelling.
A destructive wind that carries the man away.

sections.1: The hidden places of the earth

notes: The chapter has no new speaker introduction. It can be read as part of Job’s discourse or as a reflective poem within the book. The draft does not add an attribution.
The compressed mining description is difficult. The draft pictures miners hanging far from ordinary human paths.
Several mineral names have uncertain modern equivalents. Lapis lazuli, coral, crystal, pearls, and topaz are conventional approximations, not secure identifications.
The pinned Hebrew says people do not know wisdom’s worth; another familiar rendering, “way,” represents a different reading.
vocabulary: Here the Hebrew title Adonai, distinguished from LORD for the divine name.
The poem moves from searching hidden places to reverence for the Lord and turning from evil.

sections.11: I helped those who cried out

notes: The expression for Job’s prime literally speaks of his autumn days; “friendship” can also be confidential counsel.
The case Job investigated may have belonged to a person he did not know, or may itself have been unfamiliar.
The word rendered “sand” has also been understood as the phoenix, a bird associated with renewed life.
The relation between Job’s smile and the people’s confidence is difficult. The draft keeps both his reassuring smile and the light of his face.
vocabulary: Job pictures just conduct as the clothing that identified him.

notes: Job describes socially excluded people with contempt. These are his words, not an endorsement by the narrator or translator.
The rare description can picture gnawing the dry ground or fleeing into desolation. Broom roots may be food or fuel.
The read form is “my bowstring”; the written form has “his.” God is understood as the one loosening it.
The clothing and collar image is obscure. Great force may distort Job’s clothing or bind him tightly like a garment.
The final word is uncertain. “Storm” follows an interpretation of the written form; the read form is a word ordinarily associated with sound wisdom or resources.
The line can describe a ruined person reaching for help, or question striking someone already ruined.
The darkness of Job’s appearance can concern mourning or a darkened body not caused by sunlight.
vocabulary: Their cries give Job images for his own lament.

sections.13: One maker for servant and master
sections.24: If I put my trust in wealth

notes: Job’s “growth” may include his crops or his descendants.
Grinding for another man evokes servitude; the men bending over Job’s wife also carry a sexual threat. The curse’s harm to her is not softened.
The Hebrew shifts between a male and a female object, understood as the orphan and widow. Caring for them from the womb is Job’s expansive claim, not a literal chronology.
The Hebrew literally says that Job’s hand kissed his mouth. The draft describes the same gesture as kissing his hand in homage toward the heavenly lights.
“Like other people” can also be read “like Adam.”
The word for signature is a mark, taw. The passage does not give it a later religious symbolism.
The final expression can mean causing the land’s owners to die or causing them anguish.
vocabulary: Job explicitly names both a male slave and a female slave as people with a claim against him.
Job grounds his obligation in their shared creation in the womb.

sections.6: Elihu: Age alone does not make wisdom

notes: The pinned text says the three friends condemned Job despite finding no answer. It is not silently changed to condemning God.
“Many years” interprets a word that can name the great or the aged. The next clause explicitly names elders.
The image names new wineskins. The draft preserves this rather than importing the different wineskin saying from the Gospels.
vocabulary: The son of Barachel the Buzite, from the family of Ram.
Elihu attributes understanding to divine breath rather than age alone.

sections.14: God speaks in more than one way

notes: Elihu stresses that he too was formed from clay. The rare word for pressure or burden accompanies his claim that Job need not fear him.
The line may concern God not giving an account of his deeds or not answering a person’s words.
The word rendered “weapon” can also be understood in relation to a channel or river, here associated with death.
The draft follows the read forms for the whole frame of bones and for bones protruding. The original written and read forms are both preserved in the source binding.
The messenger or interpreter is not named. The subject who shows mercy and speaks of a ransom is also not explicitly identified; the draft does not assign a later religious identity.
“Sings” can also be understood as looking toward people. Verse 28 follows the read third-person forms; the written forms are first person.
vocabulary: A price or means of release from death.
Living again in contrast to descending into the pit.

notes: The opening can mean that Job is counted a liar despite his right, or that he would lie about his case. Elihu is quoting or paraphrasing Job’s position.
The object of setting the heart is uncertain: God may set his heart on himself or on a person. The withdrawal of spirit and breath follows.
The line can describe God addressing rulers as worthless, or ask whether it is proper for a person to address them that way.
The phrase may concern no further examination being needed or no appointed time for appearing before God.
The opening is understood as “if only”; it can also be read “my father.” The demand for Job to be tested is Elihu’s own severe wish.
vocabulary: The shared destination of humanity when breath is withdrawn.
An image for the harm a godless ruler brings upon a people.

sections.1: Elihu: What do your actions give God?

notes: The comparison can mean being more righteous than God or being in the right before God.
The wording shifts between “you” and “I” in the reported question. The draft keeps that movement.
God may teach people more than the animals, or teach people through the animals.
The rare term rendered “transgression” is uncertain. The verse remains part of Elihu’s explanation for Job’s speech.
vocabulary: Elihu contrasts their effect on God with their effect on other people.

sections.1: Elihu: There is more to say for God

notes: Elihu claims that one complete in knowledge is present with Job. Similar language in 37:16 refers to God.
The term rendered “weapon” has also been related to a channel or river, as in 33:18.
The term for male shrine attendants is traditionally associated with cult prostitution, but the precise role is uncertain. The draft does not assert a sexual occupation as settled.
These lines are difficult. They can concern anger, mockery, ransom, and an appeal for help, or the danger and inability of wealth to deliver.
The relation of water drops, rain, and mist is compressed; the draft retains the imagery without turning it into a technical account.
The final line about cattle and what is coming is especially obscure. The draft follows the reading that cattle announce the storm’s approach.
vocabulary: An image of relief from constriction and distress.
The deep reaches of the sea in the poem’s spatial imagery.

notes: The sealing of people’s hands can picture work being stopped so they recognize God’s work. The relation of the final words is uncertain.
The second wind expression concerns scattering winds; a specific compass direction is not certain.
The line names punishment, the land, and faithful love as possible purposes of the weather.
The skies are pictured as hard like a cast metal mirror. The ancient image is retained.
The relation between speaking and being swallowed is difficult; Elihu warns about addressing God.
Gold coming from the north is an unresolved poetic image. The draft does not identify it as a particular modern weather phenomenon.
The last verb can mean not oppressing or, with another understanding, not answering.
vocabulary: Here the description concerns God, echoing Elihu’s claim in 36:4.

notes: The earth takes shape like clay under a seal; the following garment image is compressed and its plural subject uncertain.
The claim that Job knows because he was born then is pointed irony.
The identifications Pleiades, Orion, and Bear are conventional and not certain in every detail. “Constellations” renders the obscure Mazzaroth.
The paired words can concern inward parts and the mind, or particular creatures such as the ibis and rooster. The draft follows the inward-wisdom reading.
vocabulary: Literally, gird your loins: secure clothing for demanding action.
The heavenly assembly, also named in the opening chapters.
The rain nourishes places beyond human settlement.

sections.9: Will the wild ox serve you?

notes: The ostrich’s wing and its comparison with the stork are described with rare, difficult words.
The poem’s portrayal of the ostrich is retained as poetry; it is not rewritten as a modern zoological description.
The word rendered “mane” is uncertain and has also been related to thunder.
The last clause can describe not standing still at the trumpet or not believing the trumpet’s signal.
vocabulary: The paired Hebrew names evoke the free-ranging donkey or onager.
The eagle’s young gulp blood; the image’s violence remains explicit.

sections.3: Job puts his hand over his mouth

notes: Job calls himself small or of little account; the word does not by itself mean morally vile.
Behemoth names a formidable creature. Identifying it with one particular animal, extinct or living, goes beyond what the passage settles.
The cedar-like tail and tightly woven thigh sinews are vivid but difficult; the description may also carry sexual associations.
The maker and sword clause can picture the maker bringing a sword near the creature or furnishing it with a sword.
The first question can concern capturing it while it watches or taking it by the eyes.
The Hebrew chapter continues for eight more verses. They appear here under the established public labels 41:1–8; every original record is retained.
vocabulary: The same summons to prepare for an encounter as in 38:3.
Metal supplies images for the creature’s powerful bones and limbs.

sections.25: Nothing on earth is its equal

notes: English verses 1–8 correspond to Hebrew 40:25–32; English verses 9–34 correspond to Hebrew 41:1–26.
The partners may bargain over Leviathan or feast upon it.
The draft follows the written negative, “I will not,” rather than the read form “to it.”
The “double bridle” may picture the creature’s two jaws.
The smoking pot and burning reeds form a compressed comparison.
The final expression can mean being beside oneself with terror or being purified; the fear reading fits the surrounding response.
vocabulary: A formidable creature associated elsewhere with chaotic power; the poem does not give a secure zoological classification.
The foaming deep is pictured as gray-haired.

notes: The quotation marks identify echoes of the LORD’s earlier questions. Verse 4 can also be read as Job’s own request to speak and learn.

The Hebrew supplies no object such as “myself” after the first verb. It can mean reject or retract. The second verb can mean repent, relent, or be comforted; the final phrase can mean in dust and ashes or concerning dust and ashes. The draft gives one reading without claiming the alternatives are settled.
“About me” can also mean “to me.” The LORD contrasts Job with the three friends; Elihu is not named here.
The narrator explicitly describes the calamity as what the LORD brought upon Job. The value of a kesitah is unknown; the gold ring may be an ear or nose ornament.
The daughters receive an inheritance alongside their brothers, an expressly stated feature of the ending.
vocabulary: An ancient unit of payment whose precise weight or value is uncertain.
An idiom for a life that has run its full course.
